summary: We developed COMET-X, a novel computational framework that integrates high-precision N-body numerical integration (REBOUND/IAS15) with Bayesian nested sampling inference (dynesty). COMET-X addresses the challenge of identifying transitional active asteroids by mathematically isolating weak, non-gravitational outgassing accelerations from standard astrometric observation noise and thermal radiative forces. Instead of relying on visual morphology or traditional fitting methodologies that tend to over-fit noise, COMET-X computes absolute Bayesian evidence to definitively decouple sub-surface sublimation signatures from purely gravitational trajectories. This automates candidate filtering across vast sky catalogs, guiding targeted follow-up in SPHEREx near-infrared survey imagery to detect faint cometary activity. Through a rigorous 50-run Monte Carlo validation, the pipeline successfully established a ground-based detection threshold of A₂ ≥ 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ AU/day² with a false-positive rate under 2%. This framework is highly critical for planetary defense and astrophysics. Unidentified outgassing continuously alters orbits, severely degrading multi-decade trajectory forecasts for Potentially Hazardous Asteroids (PHAs). By proactively screening Near-Earth Objects for volatile mass loss, COMET-X prevents long-term trajectory divergence and refines the bulk density and porosity estimates required to design effective kinetic impactor deflection missions.
details:
COMET-X is a computational astrophysics pipeline designed to mathematically isolate and detect weak, visually undetectable non-gravitational outgassing in Near-Earth Asteroids (NEOs). It directly challenges the traditional rigid binary taxonomy of "inert asteroids" versus "active comets" by identifying a transitional population of bodies that experience sub-surface volatile sublimation. Because this low-level outgassing rarely ejects enough dust to generate an optically detectable coma, these bodies remain completely hidden from traditional morphological telescope surveys.

At its core, the COMET-X framework couples an exact N-body dynamical integrator with a rigorous nested sampling inference engine. The N-body component calculates the heliocentric acceleration of an asteroid by integrating point-mass gravitational perturbations from the Sun and major planetary bodies, alongside an empirical non-gravitational acceleration term based on the classical Marsden cometary activity law. To compare these 3D orbital simulations with actual ground-based astronomy, the pipeline performs precise topocentric projections, converting heliocentric vectors into localized equatorial spherical coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination) relative to the position of the observing telescope.

Finally, a multivariate Gaussian log-likelihood function evaluates the simulated orbits against historical observational data. Rather than simply fitting a curve, the framework uses Bayesian evidence ($\Delta \ln Z$) to determine if adding a transverse outgassing acceleration parameter to the model is statistically demanded by the data, decoupling the sublimation signature from standard astrometric observation noise.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software

The entire COMET-X pipeline was engineered in Python 3.11.

  • Orbital Integration: We utilized the open-source REBOUND N-body framework, specifically employing the IAS15 integrator. IAS15 is an adaptive, 15th-order Gauss-Radau spacing integrator critical for maintaining machine-precision accuracy and resolving the stiff differential equations that arise during close planetary encounters without suffering from secular energy drift.
  • Bayesian Inference: The absolute marginal likelihood (Bayesian evidence) calculations were driven by the dynesty nested sampling package, which effectively maps the complex, multi-dimensional parameter space.
  • Data Ingestion & APIs: Observational astrometry was ingested via automated API queries to the Minor Planet Center (MPC) and JPL Horizons, utilizing custom rate-limiting headers (max 2 requests/second) to ensure server integrity. For photometric cross-validation, we processed Parquet light-curve files from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF DR24) and Pan-STARRS.
  • Hardware Considerations: High-throughput nested sampling sweeps are computationally intensive. Hardware thermals were actively managed to stay below a 74°C maximum load, and the researcher adhered to strict 45-minute ergonomic break intervals throughout the execution of the 50-run Monte Carlo matrix.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The primary intended impact of COMET-X is to fundamentally strengthen global planetary defense infrastructure. Unidentified outgassing poses a profound risk to precision orbit determination; it continuously imparts micro-accelerations to an asteroid that, if unmodeled, integrate secularly over multi-decade timelines. This can lead to thousands of kilometers of cross-track errors when predicting the future trajectories of Potentially Hazardous Asteroids (PHAs).

By screening uncharacterized NEO archives for hidden volatile activity, COMET-X prevents the misattribution of outgassing forces to pure gravity, thereby eliminating long-term trajectory divergence. Furthermore, identifying whether an NEO harbors volatile mass drastically refines estimates of its internal bulk density and porosity. These physical parameters are critical for modeling kinetic impactor deflection missions (such as the DART paradigm), where the target’s physical response to an impact is dictated by its internal structure.

How the Project is Creative

Traditional least-squares optimization fails to identify weak outgassing because adding extra acceleration parameters causes the models to simply over-fit the background telescope noise, resulting in false-positive detections. COMET-X creatively solves this by relying on Bayesian nested sampling, which inherently features "Occam's Razor". The 7-dimensional outgassing model occupies a significantly larger prior volume than the 6-dimensional pure gravity model. The Bayesian evidence integral automatically penalizes this extra complexity, meaning the system will aggressively reject the outgassing hypothesis unless the observational data overwhelmingly proves it exists.

Additionally, the project creatively decouples outgassing from the Yarkovsky effect purely through statistical evidence formulation. By evaluating models on highly eccentric orbits (perihelia < 1.3 AU and aphelia > 2.8 AU), the Bayesian evidence decisively isolates the Marsden sublimation curve (which drops precipitously past the 2.808 AU water-ice boundary) from Yarkovsky thermal drift (which scales continuously as $r^{-2}$).

Factors Our Team Considered

We extensively considered algorithmic stability, physical orbital constraints, and instrumental systematics during development:

  1. Rectification of Orbital Priors: We identified that previous broad uniform priors allowed the nested sampling chains to wander into non-physical regimes, selecting objects that actually orbit safely within the Main Asteroid Belt. We strictly corrected the simulated parameter domains to guarantee true Near-Earth trajectories, mathematically enforcing a perihelion boundary of $q = a(1-e) < 1.3 \text{ AU}$.
  2. Resolution of Stochastic Artifacts: During Phase 4 development, single-run tests at a low resolution ($n_{live}=50$) yielded anomalous, non-monotonic Bayes factors ($\Delta \ln Z = +2.04$ at sub-noise force levels). To resolve this sampling noise, we engineered a massive 50-run Monte Carlo injection-recovery matrix spanning 5 logarithmic force levels with 10 independent noise seeds each, raising the live points to $n_{live}=250$. This successfully eliminated the stochastic variance, suppressed the false-positive rate to < 2%, and established a highly definitive, empirical ground-based detection threshold of $A_2 \ge 5.0 \times 10^{-10} \text{ AU/day}^2$.
  3. Observatory Systematics & Photometric Aliasing: To ensure rotational brightness variations weren't mathematically aliased into the outgassing signature, we applied the standard $H-G$ magnitude system to multi-band light curves. Finally, we executed Leave-One-Observatory-Out (LOOO) cross-validation by sequentially dropping data from major contributing observatories (such as G96 Mount Lemmon and F51 Pan-STARRS 1) to definitively prove the outgassing detections were independent of any observatory-specific astrometric bias.
